h: A honeymoon souvenir you can walk around
p: Most couples bring back a fridge magnet from their honeymoon. Sir Charles Monck brought back an entire architectural style. He spent a long honeymoon in Greece in the early 1800s, fell in love with the temples of Athens, and came home determined to build his own. The hall went up between about 1810 and 1817, designed largely by Monck himself, and the precision of the stonework shows just how obsessive he was about getting it right.

The family had lived here for centuries before that. The medieval tower was their home, and in the early 1600s they added a manor house wing onto it. When the new hall was finished they moved out of the old castle, and the garden walk between the two is really a walk through the family's history.

Spring is a cracking time to visit, when the rhododendrons in the quarry garden are out and the colours against the rock faces are something else. Autumn has its own charm too. Allow at least three hours to see everything without rushing.

Morpeth is worth more than a passing glance afterwards. The Chantry houses a bagpipe museum dedicated to Northumbrian pipes, a lovely local quirk, and the town has strong links with Admiral Collingwood, Nelson's second-in-command at Trafalgar. If you've got another day, the National Trust's Wallington estate is in the countryside to the west, and Kirkharle, birthplace of Capability Brown, is close by too.
